html:
The Liangzhu culture was a Neolithic society of the Yangtze River delta in eastern China, from about 3300 to 2300 BCE. Its centre was a walled city near modern Hangzhou, and many archaeologists see it as one of the earliest states in East Asia.

The case for a state rests on what has been dug up:

  • A city of about 300 hectares inside rammed-earth walls, with a raised palace platform in the middle.
  • A system of earth dams and walls in the hills north of the city, built to control floods and water, among the oldest large waterworks in the world.
  • Rice fields and stores that could feed a large population.
  • A sharp gap between rich and poor graves. Jade, silk, ivory and lacquer appear only in elite tombs.

Liangzhu is famous for jade. Its workshops made cong, square tubes with a round hole, and bi discs, carved with a mask-like face that may be a god. Jade had no metal tools to cut it, so each piece took great labour, and the cong became a lasting form in Chinese ritual.

Its influence reached as far north as Shanxi and south to Guangdong. Its jade forms were copied by the Longshan cultures to the north, and the jade tradition flowed on into the Bronze Age of the Shang.

The culture ended around 2300 BCE, perhaps after floods. The ruins of Liangzhu City became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2019, recognised as evidence of an early Chinese civilisation older than any written record.
